title: What a Difference a Year Makes — Sir Geoffrey Vos MR, speech to the Legal Geek Conference (London, 15 October 2025)
pub: Judiciary of England and Wales (judiciary.uk) — Legal Geek Conference, London
author: Sir Geoffrey Vos

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Vos accepts selective, human-supervised deployment: AI can save time on bounded legal tasks, but outputs require verification and important source materials still require professional review. He materially extends the cluster by applying this distinction to adjudication, arguing that technical capability does not settle whether binding decisions should be automated and identifying human-rights and human-judgment boundaries requiring urgent public debate.

st.t: Court responsibility: AI requires lifecycle supervision
st.an: Vos supports the cluster’s central proposition that judicial authority should not be transferred to AI. Although he acknowledges speed and public demand for some machine-made decisions, his overall argument stresses judicial finality, distinctively human judgment, and the need for humans to remain able to check machine decisions and shape the law.
qs: If the decision is wrong, at least after an appeal,       nothing can be done about it in most cases – Parliament is       unlikely to change the law to reverse a run-of-the-mill AI-                                    2 ^L      generated judicial decision made by a machine as to personal       injury damages.
There is a potential problem if we,       as humans, become unable to second guess or even check       what the machine is suggesting or deciding.

st.t: Machine judging: Accuracy cannot establish legitimate authority
st.an: Vos accepts that speed and capability may make machine decisions attractive, but argues that these do not resolve the legitimate scope of judicial authority. He instead centres human-rights status, societal consent, challengeability and continued human influence over legal development.
qs: That is why I       have argued for some time now that we need a serious debate       now, before it is too late, to consider: (a) what human rights       people should have in the light of ever more capable AI, and       (b) what humans want, as a matter of consensus, human       judges rather than machines, to decide in the future.

It is whether a       machine-made decision can ever be properly regarded as       having been made by an “independent and impartial tribunal       established by law” for the purposes of article 6 of the       European Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental       Freedoms.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: Vos supports the cluster’s core supervised-AI framing: legal AI can save substantial time and assist with drafting, research and summarisation, but users must understand the tool, protect private data and carefully verify outputs. He also treats AI’s role in judicial decision-making as an unresolved ethical issue rather than endorsing autonomous judgment. He does not, however, argue that verification generally eliminates the efficiency gains.

st.an: Vos supports AI as an assistive tool while requiring human verification, continued engagement with important source materials, and protection of private data. He also treats AI’s role in judicial decision-making as a distinct unresolved ethical issue rather than endorsing autonomous substitution.

kp.k: Lawyers’ AI adoption has accelerated over the past year
kp.d: Vos characterises the year preceding his October 2025 speech as a shift from widespread denial of AI’s professional value to enthusiastic use of Harvey, Legora and general-purpose tools. This is his qualitative assessment, rather than a measured adoption finding; he also believes opposition to legal technology is diminishing.
qs: Last year, lawyers were generally in denial about the value of AI to their treasured profession.
I believe that the voices of those implacably opposed to the use of technology in the law are reducing in volume.

kp.k: Responsible use requires understanding, confidentiality and human verification
kp.d: Vos frames AI as a useful but potentially dangerous tool whose safety depends on its users. His three core rules for lawyers and judges require understanding what an LLM does, keeping private data out of public models, and checking outputs before any use. These are recommendations for professional practice, not a claim that AI can be relied upon autonomously.
qs: first, that you need to understand what an LLM is doing before you use it; secondly, you need to avoid putting private data into a public LLM, and thirdly, you need to check what comes out of an LLM before you use it for any purpose at all.

kp.k: Summarisation saves time without replacing substantive reading
kp.d: Vos identifies everyday summarisation as a particularly important labour-saving capability for lawyers and judges. He argues that it accelerates access to a document’s substance and reduces drudgery, while explicitly retaining the need to read important documents, precedents and judgments.
qs: An AI generated summary does not mean we can avoid reading an important document, legal precedent or judgment, but it does give us easy access to the guts of it far more quickly than was ever available before.

kp.k: Drafting and research are acceptable with careful checking
kp.d: Vos endorses AI use to generate legal advice for lawyers and judgments for judges, and sees no reason to prohibit contract drafting or legal research. He distinguishes these uses, subject to careful checking by lawyers and clients, from the harder normative question of machines making judicial decisions.
qs: Can AI properly be used to generate legal advice for lawyers and judgments for judges? Yes, of course it can.
I see no reason why AI should not be used to draft contracts and to research legal questions.
Lawyers and clients should always check what it has done carefully before using it, but that is a different issue.

kp.k: Machine adjudication could offer substantial speed advantages
kp.d: Vos uses assessment of personal injury damages against textbook authorities as an illustrative case where people might prefer machine decision-making. He suggests AI could take a couple of minutes compared with a possible two-year wait for a judicial hearing and determination. This is a hypothetical comparison supporting debate, not a reported performance study or implemented adjudication system.
qs: nobody can really tell me why AI should not be used to assess, for example, personal injury damages by reference to the numerous authorities found in the textbooks.
That task would take an AI a couple of minutes, whilst the wait for a judicial hearing and determination might be more like two years.

kp.k: Judicial finality and human qualities complicate automated decisions
kp.d: Vos gives two reasons for caution about machine adjudication: judicial decisions are generally final after appeal, and machines may never satisfactorily reproduce human emotion, idiosyncrasy, empathy and insight. His claim about future artificial general intelligence is expressly qualified rather than presented as an established technical limit.
qs: First, judicial decisions are the last resort for everyone in our society.
If the decision is wrong, at least after an appeal, nothing can be done about it in most cases

machines, even those sporting the much-vaunted artificial general intelligence when it comes, will arguably never be able completely satisfactorily to mimic a human’s emotion, idiosyncracy, empathy and insight.

kp.k: Automated adjudication could weaken human influence on legal development
kp.d: Vos’s third concern is long-term: machine decisions reflect intelligence at a particular point without developing human thought. He warns conditionally that, if humans become unable to question or check machine decisions, their capacity to influence the future evolution of law could diminish.
qs: with an AI judicial decision, you will be getting something generated from the state of intelligence at a given point in time, without the application of developing human thought.
There is a potential problem if we, as humans, become unable to second guess or even check what the machine is suggesting or deciding.
In that situation, it might be very difficult for human thought processes to influence the law of the future in the way that many people might think remained appropriate.

kp.k: Machine decisions raise unresolved Article 6 questions
kp.d: Vos calls for immediate debate about human rights under increasingly capable AI. He identifies whether machine-made decisions can satisfy Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms as a critical unresolved legal question, reporting disagreement rather than asserting a settled legal answer.
qs: It is whether a machine-made decision can ever be properly regarded as having been made by an “independent and impartial tribunal established by law” for the purposes of article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms.
Some think so, but many more think not.

kp.k: Society should decide which judgments remain human
kp.d: Vos recommends building consensus about which decisions should be reserved for human judges and whether individuals should have a choice between machine and human adjudication. He raises machine sentencing and judges consulting one or several AI tools as questions, not endorsed policies. He separately asserts that Chinese judges already routinely use AI in sentencing.
qs: What do we, as humans, want human judges rather than machines, to decide in the future?
What do we, as a society, want machines to decide about our lives in preference to human judges, and ought we to have a choice.
In China, judges already routinely use AI in that process.

kp.k: Digital justice should expand access with professional participation
kp.d: Vos presents responsible, effective and safe AI use alongside continued development of a Digital Justice System as complementary objectives. He links efficient, economic and expeditious online, out-of-court dispute resolution to greater access to justice, and stresses the need to bring the entire legal community along. This is a stated programme of reform rather than evidence of achieved access improvements.
qs: First, we want to see that AI is used responsibly, effectively and safely in legal systems and processes.

Secondly, I think we all want to see the continuing creation of an efficient, economic and expeditious Digital Justice System to resolve people’s many legal disputes online and out of court and, thereby, to create greater access to justice for all.
In delivering these two admirable objectives, we must make sure that we bring the entire legal community with us.

kp.k: International private-law alignment aims to support digital trade
kp.d: In a separate digital-assets initiative, Vos reports that the International Jurisdiction Taskforce began in 2025 with legal experts and central bankers from Japan, the EU, the USA, the UK, France, Singapore and Australia. Its early-stage work will compare relevant private laws and regulatory environments and examine broader applicability of UKJT statements on digital assets as property, securitisation and insolvency. He distinguishes English from UK law, New York from USA law, and rejects treating EU private law as the relevant unit; the aim is fewer legal impediments to cross-border on-chain transactions, not an AI-specific finding.
qs: The IJT project is at an early stage, but it will start by looking at the differences between those private laws and their fast-changing regulatory environments as of today.
They will then try to see how and whether the UKJT’s legal statements on digital assets as property, securitisation of digital assets, and digital assets in insolvency are applicable more broadly.
I hope the IJT will be another brick in the wall towards the widespread adoption of global digital trading.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Vos describes accelerating lawyer adoption, immediate labour-saving uses, and the possibility—but not unconditional endorsement—of AI judicial decision-making.
pts.d: Sir Geoffrey Vos claims that lawyers moved from general denial of AI's value to extensive use over the preceding year. He describes AI summarisation as saving time and drudgery while not replacing the reading of important documents. He endorses AI-assisted contract drafting and legal research, subject to checking, and says AI can generate legal advice and judgments. Separately, he suggests that assessing personal injury damages could take AI minutes rather than the potentially years-long wait for a judicial hearing and determination. He does not present this as sufficient reason to delegate adjudication: he raises concerns about finality, human empathy and insight, and the future development of law if humans cannot check machine decisions. He reports that Chinese judges already routinely use AI in sentencing, without claiming that sentencing is wholly automated. Whether people should choose machine or human adjudication, and whether machine decisions satisfy Article 6, remain open questions in his account. An efficient digital justice system that resolves disputes online and out of court to expand access to justice is an expressed objective, not a demonstrated AI outcome.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on Vos's professional observations, practical illustrations and legal-ethical reasoning, rather than reported empirical testing.
pts.d: Speaking as Master of the Rolls and Head of Civil Justice in England and Wales, Vos offers a qualitative account of changing professional attitudes. He names AI products being used and points to document summarisation as a familiar practical example, but supplies no adoption survey, sample, productivity measurement or benchmark. The minutes-versus-years comparison for personal injury damages is an illustrative prospective comparison between AI task execution and waiting for judicial resolution, not a reported controlled study. His statement about Chinese sentencing practice has no accompanying citation or case details. Concerns about machine adjudication are supported by arguments about the finality of judgments, distinctively human qualities and legal development; Article 6 supplies a legal framework for a question rather than a resolved finding. The access-to-justice discussion states a policy aspiration without measuring outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Adoption and assistance claims concern October 2025 and the preceding year; autonomous adjudication raises immediate policy questions and longer-term, explicitly conditional risks.
pts.d: The speech was delivered on 15 October 2025, making the adoption comparison approximately 2024–2025. Vos presents summarisation and drafting or research assistance as current capabilities. Safe use requires understanding what an LLM does, keeping private data out of public LLMs and verifying outputs before any use; important source documents still need reading. The personal injury example uses conditional language and offers no implementation date. His prediction about machines' inability fully to mimic human qualities is qualified by 'arguably' and extends to future artificial general intelligence. The risk to legal development is conditional on humans losing the ability to check or second-guess machine decisions and is framed over generations. He calls for debate now, before decisions about machine adjudication become entrenched, but gives no timetable for deployment or digital justice outcomes.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Lawyers, judges and clients face changed working practices; litigants and the wider public face questions about speed, human adjudication, rights and access to justice.
pts.d: Lawyers and judges are described as gaining faster access to document contents and relief from routine work, while retaining responsibility for understanding tools and checking outputs. Clients share the stated need to check AI-assisted drafting and research before use. Personal injury litigants illustrate the potential speed advantage of machine assessment; criminal defendants illustrate unresolved questions about preferences for human versus machine sentencing. The wider public is affected by the legitimacy and finality of adjudication, preservation of human judgment, and the future development of law. People with legal disputes are the intended beneficiaries of the proposed accessible digital justice system. Vos does not differentiate effects by firm size or market tier and makes no specific prediction about staffing, job losses, fees or provider competition.
